slides.narration: Welcome. Today's poem is For Anne Gregory by W. B. Yeats. It is a short conversation between an older man and a young woman about a big question: can a beautiful person be loved for who she really is? Please read it in First Flight now, aloud, twice. We will not repeat its lines here. Instead we will follow the debate.

slides.heading: How to read this poem
bullets: Read it aloud twice from *First Flight*; notice who speaks each stanza.
Ask: what does the older speaker warn? how does Anne answer? who has the last word?
Then ask: what is the poem saying about beauty and love?
In answers, explain in your own words; never copy lines.
slides.narration: Read the poem aloud twice, and notice who is speaking in each stanza. Ask what the older speaker warns, how Anne answers, and who has the last word. Then ask what the poem is saying about beauty and love. In the exam, explain in your own words. Copying lines earns no marks.

slides.narration: William Butler Yeats was an Irish poet and dramatist who lived from eighteen sixty-five to nineteen thirty-nine. In nineteen twenty-three he received the Nobel Prize in Literature. With his friend Lady Gregory he helped found the Abbey Theatre in Dublin. Anne Gregory was Lady Gregory's granddaughter, and this poem is addressed to her.

slides.heading: The poem at a glance

rows: a dialogue in three six-line stanzas; lines 2, 4 and 6 rhyme
an older man (stanzas 1 and 3) and Anne (stanza 2)
whether a beautiful young woman can be loved for her true self
her golden hair as honey-coloured fortress walls
outer beauty versus inner worth; only divine love is unconditional

visual.alt: Table of the poem at a glance: a dialogue in three six-line stanzas, an older man and Anne as speakers, the question of being loved for one's true self, her hair as honey-coloured fortress walls, the theme of outer beauty versus inner worth, and an affectionate tone that becomes philosophical.

slides.narration: Here is the poem at a glance. It is a dialogue in three six-line stanzas. An older man speaks first and last; Anne speaks in the middle. The question is whether a beautiful young woman can be loved for her true self. The key image is her golden hair as fortress walls. The tone is affectionate, then philosophical.

slides.heading: Stanza 1: the warning
slides.body_md: In SOYL's words: the older speaker tells Anne that the suitors who fall hopelessly for her will never love her purely for herself. What captivates them is her golden hair, which he pictures as honey-coloured walls of a fortress around her ears.
slides.narration: In the first stanza, the older speaker gives Anne a warning. The suitors who fall hopelessly for her, he says, will never love her purely for herself. What captivates them is her beautiful golden hair. He pictures it as honey-coloured walls of a fortress around her ears. It is affectionate, but it is also a warning.

slides.heading: Stanza 2: Anne's answer
slides.body_md: In SOYL's words: Anne answers that she can simply dye her hair, perhaps brown, black or bright orange-red, so that suitors will have to value her for her true self. Her reply is quick, practical and a little playful.
slides.narration: In the second stanza, Anne answers back. She can simply dye her hair, she says, perhaps brown, black or bright orange-red. Then suitors would have to value her for her true self. Her reply is quick, practical and a little playful. She believes beauty can be removed like a coat, leaving the real person behind.

slides.heading: Check: Anne's solution
slides.narration: Your turn. What does Anne suggest she could do about the problem? Choose the best answer.

slides.heading: Stanza 3: the last word
slides.body_md: In SOYL's words: the older speaker replies that just the night before he heard an elderly, devout man announce that he had found scripture proving that God alone could love a person purely for herself, and not for her golden hair.
slides.narration: In the third stanza, the older speaker has the last word. Just the night before, he says, he heard an elderly, devout man announce that he had found scripture proving something: that God alone could love a person purely for herself, and not for her golden hair. The conversation rises from hair to the soul.

slides.heading: What the ending means
slides.body_md: Human love, the poem suggests, is always partly drawn by appearance. A new hair colour would only create a new surface to admire. Only divine love is completely unconditional.
slides.narration: What does the ending mean? Human love, the poem suggests, is always partly drawn by appearance. If Anne dyed her hair, suitors would simply admire the new colour, or some other feature. Only divine love sees the soul and ignores the surface. That is the wiser, sadder truth the older speaker offers.

visual.alt: Table comparing the two speakers: the older speaker is experienced, believes beauty hides the true self, offers no earthly solution and speaks teasingly then philosophically; Anne is young and hopeful, believes beauty can be changed, proposes dyeing her hair, and speaks confidently.

slides.narration: Put the two speakers side by side. The older speaker is experienced. He thinks beauty hides the true self, and that God alone loves unconditionally. Anne is young and hopeful. She thinks beauty can be changed, so she will dye her hair. The poem lets us smile at both, but it gives the last word to age.

slides.heading: Themes and message
bullets: **Outer beauty versus inner worth:** people are drawn by looks more than character.
**The limits of human love:** it always notices appearance.
**Divine love:** God alone loves unconditionally.
**Youth and age:** hopeful plans meet experienced wisdom.
slides.narration: The themes follow. People are drawn by outer beauty more than inner worth. Human love always notices appearance. Only divine love is unconditional. And youth meets age: a hopeful plan meets experienced wisdom. In answers, state a theme and support it with what each speaker says, in your own words.

slides.narration: Now the devices. A metaphor turns Anne's hair into honey-coloured fortress walls. A refrain closes each stanza with nearly the same idea. The poem is a dialogue between two speakers. Imagery gives the hair its honey colour. And rhyme falls on the second, fourth and sixth lines. The examples on the right are our own sentences.

slides.heading: Worked point: the fortress metaphor
slides.body_md: Why call hair the walls of a fortress?
bullets: **Clue 1:** fortress walls protect what is inside.
**Clue 2:** they also stop outsiders from getting in.
**Meaning:** Anne's beauty guards her, and blocks suitors' view of her true self.
**Why it matters:** the image contains the whole argument of the poem.
slides.narration: Here is a worked point. Why call hair the walls of a fortress? Fortress walls protect what is inside, but they also stop outsiders from getting in. So Anne's beauty guards her, and also blocks suitors from seeing her true self. That one image contains the whole argument of the poem.

slides.heading: Tone
slides.body_md: Affectionate and lightly teasing at first; Anne's reply is confident and playful; the last stanza is reflective and philosophical.
slides.narration: Listen to the tone. The older speaker begins affectionately, lightly teasing Anne, like an old family friend. Anne's reply is confident and playful. In the last stanza the tone becomes reflective and philosophical. A light conversation about hair turns into a serious thought about love.

slides.heading: Worked example: a 40–50 word answer
slides.body_md: *Question:* Why does the older speaker doubt Anne's suitors?
bullets: **Point:** he thinks they love her looks, not her self.
**View (own words):** her golden hair captivates them, like fortress walls.
**Link:** human love notices appearance; God's love alone does not.

**Model (44 words):** *The older speaker believes Anne's admirers are dazzled by her lovely golden hair, which he imagines as fortress walls. They see her beauty, not her character. He adds that human affection always notices looks, and that God alone can love someone purely for herself.*

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: The older speaker warns Anne that suitors will love her golden hair, not her.
He pictures her hair as honey-coloured fortress walls.
Anne replies that she could dye it, so they would love her true self.
He answers that God alone can love a person purely for herself.
Message: human love notices beauty; only divine love is unconditional. Read the poem in *First Flight*.

**W. B. Yeats** (1865–1939) was an Irish poet and dramatist, a leader of the Irish literary revival and winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature (1923). With Lady Augusta Gregory he helped found Dublin's Abbey Theatre. *For Anne Gregory* is addressed to Lady Gregory's granddaughter.

sections.heading: 3. Themes and message
sections.body_md:
- **Outer beauty versus inner worth:** people are drawn by appearance more than by character.
- **The limits of human love:** it always notices looks; changing them only creates a new surface.
- **Divine love:** God alone loves unconditionally.
- **Youth and age:** Anne's hopeful plan meets the speaker's experienced, gently ironic wisdom.

sections.heading: 4. Form, devices and imagery
sections.body_md:
**Form:** a dialogue in three six-line stanzas; the older speaker has stanzas 1 and 3, Anne stanza 2. Rhyme falls on lines 2, 4 and 6 of each stanza.

**Devices:** metaphor (hair as honey-coloured fortress walls); refrain (nearly the same idea ends each stanza); imagery (the honey colour); dialogue.

questions.passage_md: The poem opens with an older speaker addressing a young woman, Anne Gregory. He tells her, half teasing and half serious, that the suitors who fall hopelessly for her will never love her purely for herself. What draws them is her beautiful golden hair, which he pictures as honey-toned walls of a fortress around her ears. The image is affectionate but also a warning. Her beauty is so striking that it stands in front of her, like a defence, and admirers may never get past it to the person inside.

answer.model_answer_md:
Coole, evening

Mr Yeats was in one of his teasing moods today. He told me, quite seriously, that no admirer would ever value me for myself, because they would all be dazzled by my hair. He even called it the walls of a fortress! I laughed and said I would simply dye it dark brown, jet black or even carrot-orange, and then we would see. He smiled and said an old churchman had found proof that God alone could love someone purely for herself. I pretended to be cross, but I keep thinking about it. Do people really see me, or only my hair? I hope that one day someone will prove him wrong.

answer.model_answer_md: I partly agree with the older speaker. In For Anne Gregory, he argues that human love is always drawn by appearance, and much experience supports him. First impressions depend on looks, and admirers often fade when beauty does. However, I think he is too pessimistic. Many people come to love others deeply for their kindness, humour and loyalty, long after appearance stops mattering. Parents love children whatever they look like, and lifelong friends see beyond the surface. Perhaps the poem's real point is that perfectly unconditional love, which never notices appearance at all, is beyond human beings. In that sense the speaker is right. answer.model_answer_md: Yeats shapes For Anne Gregory as a dialogue in three six-line stanzas. answer.model_answer_md: The message of For Anne Gregory seems even more relevant today. The older speaker warns Anne that admirers will be captivated by her beautiful hair rather than by her character. On social media, appearance is everything: filters smooth faces, and likes reward looks far more than ideas or kindness.
